doc.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Vocalese and Lambert, Hendricks and Ross
title: Moody's Mood for Love inspires Four Brothers and vocalese
summary: Hearing King Pleasure led him to write Four Brothers and lyricize orchestral arrangements, leading to Sing a Song of Basie.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: That inspired me. When I heard King Pleasure do that, I immediately wrote Four Brothers.

Yeah. I had been thinking about it, because I could sing the whole arrangement. I knew all the solos and all of the – the whole arrangement. I used to sing it to myself. When I heard Moody’s Mood for Love, I said, that’s the answer. I don’t have to stop at 8 bars, or I don’t have to stop at 32 bars. I can go on and on and on and on. That’s when I did that. I was inspired by that song.
So what did this really do for your concept of music from that point on?

I started to lyricize orchestral arrangements, which is what Leonard Feather came to call “vocalese.” That’s when we did Sing a Song of Basie. Then that’s when we recorded that. We had 13 voices. They were terrible. They were the Dave Lambert Singers. One of them was Annie Ross. They were so bad that we just took Annie and multi-tracked four times each to get the 12 horns in the Basie band – four trumpets, three trombones, and five reeds. So that’s how that came about.
